name: GNU C Library
summary: A broad GNU implementation of the C library and operating-system-facing interfaces with symbol-versioned ABI support, dynamic loading, thread-local runtime state, and extensive platform integration.

features.name: Symbol-versioned library ABI
features.description: glibc maintains exported interfaces through ABI lists, symbol versioning support, and compatibility mechanisms in the source tree, allowing multiple historical symbol versions to coexist at the library boundary.
benefits: Supports compatibility with programs built against earlier glibc interfaces
Makes library evolution explicit at the binary symbol boundary
costs: Historical ABI commitments increase maintenance surface
Symbol version selection complicates linking and debugging

features.name: Dynamic loader and relocation
features.description: glibc includes the ELF dynamic linker, relocation, symbol lookup, and shared-object loading implementation, forming a runtime boundary between executable objects and their loaded dependencies.
benefits: Allows programs to share libraries and resolve dependencies at load time
Separates executable composition from the complete set of runtime objects
costs: Runtime behavior depends on loader paths, object metadata, and relocation state
Dynamic dependencies add deployment and compatibility failure modes

features.name: Thread-local and process runtime
features.description: The glibc source contains NPTL thread creation and cleanup, thread-control-block and TLS layout support, allocator implementation, and process-facing library subsystems that coordinate with the operating system.
benefits: Provides standardized process and thread services through one libc boundary
Supports per-thread state and concurrent runtime operations
costs: Thread, TLS, and allocator lifecycles add cross-layer state transitions
Platform and kernel integration expands the implementation and testing surface

mathematical_views.question: How can a library evolve while preserving the set of historical symbol contracts required by existing binaries?
assumptions: A binary interface is modeled as symbols paired with version labels and calling contracts
Compatibility is considered at symbol resolution and interface availability, not complete behavioral equivalence
The view abstracts compiler and processor-specific calling convention details

mathematical_views.question: How do executable objects, shared libraries, relocations, and thread-local runtime state form a process during startup and loading?
assumptions: Object files are vertices and load-time dependency or relocation requirements are directed edges
The graph describes loader composition and omits scheduling and application-level behavior
TLS and allocator state are modeled as process lifecycle resources rather than ordinary graph vertices

benefits: Historical binaries can resolve maintained symbol contracts
costs: ABI compatibility creates long-lived maintenance obligations

benefits: Shared libraries reduce duplicated deployed code
costs: Loader paths and runtime dependencies increase deployment complexity

benefits: Common process and concurrency services are available through libc
costs: Cross-layer thread and TLS state expands lifecycle reasoning
